claim: Buttonhead (Btd) is the Drosophila homolog of mammalian Sp8 transcription factor.
source: In this study, we investigate the role of the Sp family transcription factor Buttonhead (Btd) in type II NB lineage development. Btd is a homolog of mammalian Sp8 (Treichel et al., 2003; Estella and Mann, 2010).
evidence: The manuscript directly states this relationship and cites supporting literature (Treichel et al., 2003; Estella and Mann, 2010).

claim: Loss of Btd leads to elimination of mature INPs in type II neuroblast lineages.
source: We show that the loss of Btd leads to elimination of mature INPs due to premature differentiation of INPs into terminally dividing ganglion mother cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: RNAi knockdown of Btd using pntP1-GAL4 led to a complete elimination of mature INPs in about 50% of type II NB lineages.
source: Interestingly, RNAi knockdown of Btd using the type II NB lineage-specific pntP1-GAL4 (named as GAL414−94 previously) (Zhu et al., 2011) as a driver led to a complete elimination of mature INPs in about 50% of type II NB lineages (Figure 1B–B′,G–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 1G-H showing the percentage of lineages affected.

claim: All btdXG81 mutant and 90% of btdXA mutant type II NB clones failed to generate any mature INPs.
source: Consistent with the Btd RNAi knockdown, all btdXG81 mutant and 90% of btdXA mutant type II NB clones failed to generate any mature INPs except for 4–6 Ase+ Dpn− cells (Figure 1D–F′,G–H).
evidence: This is quantitative data from mutant analysis shown in Figure 1D-H.

claim: About 40% of btd mutant type II NBs ectopically express Ase.
source: Moreover, about 40% of btd mutant type II NBs ectopically express Ase, making them appear as type I NB lineages (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is quantitative data from mutant analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Mammalian Sp8 can rescue the loss of mature INPs in btd mutant type II NB clones.
source: Remarkably, the loss of INPs in btd mutant clones can be similarly rescued by the expression of mouse Sp8 or Drosophila Btd (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting that mammalian Sp8 could have a conserved role in promoting the generation of transient amplifying INPs.
evidence: This is experimental data showing functional rescue, presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A normal type II NB lineage contains about 20–30 (26.9 ± 4.1, mean ± SD) Ase+ Dpn+ mature INPs.
source: A normal type II NB lineage contains 2–3 Ase− immature INPs, 2–3 Ase+ immature INP, and about 20–30 (26.9 ± 4.1, mean ± SD) Ase+ Dpn+ mature INPs (Figure 1A–A′,C–C′,G).
evidence: This is quantitative data describing wild-type lineages, shown in Figure 1A-C' and quantified in Figure 1G.

claim: R9D11-CD4-tdTomato is expressed in Ase+ immature INPs and mature INPs but not in Ase− immature INPs in normal type II NB lineages.
source: In normal type II NB lineages, R9D11-CD4-tdTomato is first turned on in Ase+ immature INPs and becomes stronger as INPs mature (Figure 2A–A′), which is similar to R9D11-mCD8-GFP (Zhu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is observational data from immunostaining shown in Figure 2A-A' and cited from previous work.

claim: Mira is expressed in all NBs as well as INPs but not (or very weakly) in GMCs.
source: Mira is expressed in all NBs as well as INPs but not (or very weakly) in GMCs (Figure 2—–figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observational data from immunostaining shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In Btd RNAi knockdown type II NB lineages without mature INPs, R9D11-CD4-tdTomato was expressed in Ase+ daughter cells next to the Ase− immature INPs but its overall expression was much weaker than that in normal type II NB lineages.
source: In Btd RNAi knockdown type II NB lineages without mature INPs, we found that R9D11-CD4-tdTomato was expressed in Ase+ daughter cells next to the Ase− immature INPs but its overall expression was much weaker than that in normal type II NB lineages (Figure 2B–B′,I).
evidence: This is observational and quantitative data shown in Figure 2B-B' and quantified in Figure 2I.

claim: Ase− immature INPs still differentiate into Ase+ immature INP in the absence of Btd.
source: The expression of R9D11-CD4-tdTomato and Mira suggests that Ase− immature INPs still differentiate into Ase+ immature INP in the absence of Btd as in wild-type type II NB lineages (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is an inference based on marker expression data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ase+ immature INPs never become pH3-positive in wild-type type II NB lineages.
source: Immunostaining with the mitotic marker phospho-histone 3 (pH3) showed that unlike Ase+ immature INPs, which never become pH3-positive (Figure 2C–C′), some Ase+ daughter cells generated in both Btd RNAi knockdown type II NB lineages without mature INPs (Figure 2D–D′) and btd mutant type II NB lineages became mitotically active (Figure 2E–E′).
evidence: This is observational data from immunostaining shown in Figure 2C-E'.

claim: Some Ase+ daughter cells in Btd RNAi knockdown and btd mutant type II NB lineages become mitotically active.
source: Immunostaining with the mitotic marker phospho-histone 3 (pH3) showed that unlike Ase+ immature INPs, which never become pH3-positive (Figure 2C–C′), some Ase+ daughter cells generated in both Btd RNAi knockdown type II NB lineages without mature INPs (Figure 2D–D′) and btd mutant type II NB lineages became mitotically active (Figure 2E–E′).
evidence: This is observational data from pH3 immunostaining shown in Figure 2D-E'.

claim: The pH3 positive cells in btd mutant lineages were always the furthest from the Ase− immature INPs among the Ase+ daughter cells.
source: However, the pH3 positive cells were always the furthest from the Ase− immature INPs among the Ase+ daughter cells (Figure 2D–D′), suggesting that the Ase+ daughter cells divide terminally like GMCs.
evidence: This is observational data from Figure 2D-D' used to infer terminal division behavior.

claim: Mature INPs form a Mira crescent at metaphase.
source: Consistently, unlike in mature INPs, which form a Mira crescent at metaphase (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), we did not observe any Mira crescents in the Ase+ daughter cells at metaphase (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observational data from immunostaining shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: No Mira crescents were observed in the Ase+ daughter cells at metaphase in btd mutant lineages.
source: Consistently, unlike in mature INPs, which form a Mira crescent at metaphase (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), we did not observe any Mira crescents in the Ase+ daughter cells at metaphase (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observational data from immunostaining shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In normal type II NBs lineages, Pros is expressed in the cytoplasm of Ase+ immature INPs and mature INPs and in the nucleus of GMCs and post-mitotic neurons, but not in type II NBs or Ase− immature INPs.
source: In normal type II NBs lineages, Pros is expressed in the cytoplasm of Ase+ immature INPs and mature INPs and in the nucleus of GMCs and post-mitotic neurons, but not in type II NBs or Ase− immature INPs (Figure 2F–F′).
evidence: This is observational data from Pros immunostaining shown in Figure 2F-F'.

claim: Nuclear Pros was expressed in all Ase+ daughter cells and in Ase− immature INPs generated in Btd RNAi knockdown or btd mutant type II NB lineages.
source: Interestingly, immunostaining of Pros showed that nuclear Pros was expressed not only in all Ase+ daughter cells but also in Ase− immature INPs generated in Btd RNAi knockdown or btd mutant type II NB lineages (Figure 2G–H′).
evidence: This is observational data from Pros immunostaining shown in Figure 2G-H'.

claim: Pros promotes cell cycle exit and GMC differentiation.
source: Given that Pros promotes cell cycle exit and GMC differentiation and that forced expression of Pros is sufficient to eliminate INPs in type II NB lineages (Li and Vaessin, 2000; Choksi et al., 2006; Bayraktar et al., 2010), the ectopic expression of nuclear Pros in immature INPs resulting from the loss of Btd very likely promotes the premature differentiation of Ase+ immature INPs into GMCs and cell cycle exit, leading to the loss of mature INPs (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Li and Vaessin, 2000; Choksi et al., 2006; Bayraktar et al., 2010).

claim: Forced expression of Pros is sufficient to eliminate INPs in type II NB lineages.
source: Given that Pros promotes cell cycle exit and GMC differentiation and that forced expression of Pros is sufficient to eliminate INPs in type II NB lineages (Li and Vaessin, 2000; Choksi et al., 2006; Bayraktar et al., 2010), the ectopic expression of nuclear Pros in immature INPs resulting from the loss of Btd very likely promotes the premature differentiation of Ase+ immature INPs into GMCs and cell cycle exit, leading to the loss of mature INPs (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Li and Vaessin, 2000; Choksi et al., 2006; Bayraktar et al., 2010).

claim: The ectopic expression of nuclear Pros in immature INPs resulting from the loss of Btd promotes the premature differentiation of Ase+ immature INPs into GMCs and cell cycle exit.
source: Given that Pros promotes cell cycle exit and GMC differentiation and that forced expression of Pros is sufficient to eliminate INPs in type II NB lineages (Li and Vaessin, 2000; Choksi et al., 2006; Bayraktar et al., 2010), the ectopic expression of nuclear Pros in immature INPs resulting from the loss of Btd very likely promotes the premature differentiation of Ase+ immature INPs into GMCs and cell cycle exit, leading to the loss of mature INPs (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed ectopic Pros expression and known Pros function, illustrated in Figure 2J.

claim: Btd is responsible for the suppression of Pros in immature INPs.
source: These results also reveal that it is Btd that is responsible for the suppression of Pros in immature INPs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ectopic Pros expression observed when Btd is lost.

claim: The elimination of mature INPs resulting from the Btd RNAi knockdown was nearly fully rescued by removing one wild-type copy of pros.
source: Remarkably, the elimination of mature INPs resulting from the Btd RNAi knockdown was nearly fully rescued even just by removing one wild-type copy of pros (Figure 3A–D′,I–J).
evidence: This is experimental rescue data shown in Figure 3A-D' and quantified in Figure 3I-J.

claim: Knockdown of Btd in pros17 or pros10419 heterozygous mutant animals no longer led to an obvious loss of mature INPs.
source: Unlike Btd RNAi knockdown in wild-type background, which resulted in a completely elimination of mature INPs in about 50% of type II NB lineages (Figure 1B–B′,G–H, Figure 3B–B′,I–J), knockdown of Btd in pros17 or pros10419 heterozygous mutant animals no longer led to an obvious loss of mature INPs (Figure 3D–D′,I–J, and data not shown), although type II NB lineages develop normally in pros17 or pros10419 heterozygous mutant animals (Figure 3C–C′,I–J, and data not shown).
evidence: This is experimental rescue data shown in Figure 3D-D' and quantified in Figure 3I-J.

claim: The loss of INPs in btd mutant clones was largely rescued when btd mutant type II NB clones were generated in pros17 heterozygous mutant background.
source: Similarly, the loss of INPs in btd mutant clones was also largely rescued when btd mutant type II NB clones were generated in pros17 heterozygous mutant background (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is experimental rescue data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pros RNAi knockdown rescued the loss of INPs resulting from the loss of Btd.
source: Consistent with the rescue in pros heterozygous mutant animals, Pros RNAi knockdown also rescued the loss of INPs resulting from the loss of Btd (Figure 3E–H′, K–L, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is experimental rescue data shown in Figure 3E-H', K-L and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pros RNAi knockdown led to overproliferation of mature INPs.
source: Pros RNAi knockdown led to overproliferation of mature INPs as observed in pros mutant type II NB clones (Figure 3G–G′,K, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) (Bowman et al., 2008).
evidence: This is observational data shown in Figure 3G-G', K and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, consistent with cited literature (Bowman et al., 2008).

claim: When Pros was knocked down in btd mutant type II NB clones, mature INPs were rescued in all btd mutant clones.
source: When Pros was knocked down in btd mutant type II NB clones, mature INPs were rescued in all btd mutant clones (Figure 3H–H′,L).
evidence: This is experimental rescue data shown in Figure 3H-H' and quantified in Figure 3L.

claim: In about 70% of btd mutant type II NB clones, Pros RNAi knockdown led to a similar mature INP overproliferation as in wild-type clones.
source: In about 70% of btd mutant type II NB clones, Pros RNAi knockdown led to a similar mature INP overproliferation as in wild-type clones.
evidence: This is quantitative data from the rescue experiments.

claim: Removing one wild-type copy of pros or knocking down Pros suppressed the ectopic Ase expression in all btd mutant type II NBs.
source: Interestingly, removing one wild-type copy of pros or knocking down Pros not only rescued the loss of mature INPs but also suppressed the ectopic Ase expression in all btd mutant type II NBs (Figure 3H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the ectopic Ase expression in btd mutant type II NBs also results from the ectopic expression of nuclear Pros in immature INPs.
evidence: This is observational data from rescue experiments shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ectopic nuclear Pros in immature INPs is responsible for the loss of mature INPs.
source: Results from these rescue experiments demonstrate that the ectopic nuclear Pros in immature INPs is indeed responsible for the loss of mature INPs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments with pros reduction.

claim: Knockdown of Btd using erm-GAL4 (III) did not result in any obvious loss of mature INPs in type II NB lineages.
source: However, knockdown of Btd using either erm-GAL4 (III) (Figure 4A–B′′,E) or erm-GAL4 (II) (Figure 4C–D′′,F) did not result in any obvious loss of mature INPs in type II NB lineages.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4A-B'' and quantified in Figure 4E.

claim: Knockdown of Btd using erm-GAL4 (II) did not result in any obvious loss of mature INPs in type II NB lineages.
source: However, knockdown of Btd using either erm-GAL4 (III) (Figure 4A–B′′,E) or erm-GAL4 (II) (Figure 4C–D′′,F) did not result in any obvious loss of mature INPs in type II NB lineages.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4C-D'' and quantified in Figure 4F.

claim: Multicellular btd mutant INP clones were comparable to wild-type INP clones.
source: In line with these RNAi knockdown results, we were able to recover multicellular btd mutant INP clones that were comparable to wild-type INP clones (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) while we generated btd mutant type II NB clones, indicating that btd mutant INPs were still able to divide multiple rounds like wild-type INPs and did not prematurely differentiate into GMCs.
evidence: This is observational data from clonal analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Btd likely suppresses Pros expression only in newly born Ase− immature INPs but not in immature INPs at later developmental stages or mature INPs.
source: These data suggest that Btd likely suppresses Pros expression only in newly born Ase− immature INPs but not in immature INPs at later developmental stages or mature INPs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the stage-specific knockdown experiments using different GAL4 drivers.

claim: PntP1 is expressed in type II NBs as well as Ase− and Ase+ immature INPs.
source: We showed previously that PntP1 is expressed in type II NBs as well as Ase− and Ase+ immature INPs (Figure 5A–A′′) (Zhu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is observational data shown in Figure 5A-A'' and cited from previous work (Zhu et al., 2011).

claim: Inhibiting PntP1 activity results in ectopic Ase expression in type II NBs and elimination of INPs.
source: Inhibiting PntP1 activity results in ectopic Ase expression in type II NBs and elimination of INPs (Zhu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from previous work (Zhu et al., 2011).

claim: PntP1 was expressed at reduced levels in most btd mutant type II NB lineages without the ectopic Ase expression.
source: Immunostaining of PntP1 showed that PntP1 was expressed at reduced levels in most btd mutant type II NB lineages without the ectopic Ase expression (Figure 5B–B′).
evidence: This is observational data from PntP1 immunostaining shown in Figure 5B-B'.

claim: The reduction of PntP1 in btd mutant type II NBs is about 10% in the NBs and 50% in the immature INPs.
source: The reduction is about 10% in the NBs and 50% in the immature INPs (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This is quantitative data shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: In btd mutant type II NB lineages with the ectopic Ase expression in the NB, PntP1 was largely abolished in both the NBs and their progeny.
source: However, in btd mutant type II NB lineages with the ectopic Ase expression in the NB, PntP1 was largely abolished in both the NBs and their progeny (Figure 5C–C′,E–F).
evidence: This is observational and quantitative data shown in Figure 5C-C', E-F.

claim: PntP1 was detected in the Ase+ daughter cells next to the Ase− immature INPs in btd mutant clones without ectopic Ase expression in the NB.
source: In those btd mutant clones, PntP1 was also detected in the Ase+ daughter cells next to the Ase− immature INPs (Figure 5B–B′), providing additional evidence to support that Ase− immature INPs still differentiate into Ase+ immature INPs in the absence of Btd.
evidence: This is observational data shown in Figure 5B-B' used to support the differentiation claim.

claim: Expressing UAS-pntP1 resulted in higher expression of PntP1 in btd mutant type II NB clones than that in neighboring btd heterozygous mutant type II NB lineages and suppressed the ectopic Ase expression in all btd mutant type II NBs.
source: Our results showed that expressing UAS-pntP1 resulted in higher expression of PntP1 in btd mutant type II NB clones than that in neighboring btd heterozygous mutant type II NB lineages and suppressed the ectopic Ase expression in all btd mutant type II NBs (n = 12) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from rescue experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Expressing UAS-pntP1 failed to rescue mature INPs or suppress the ectopic nuclear Pros in Ase− immature INPs or Ase+ daughter cells in the majority of btd mutant clones.
source: However, unlike reducing Pros expression, which rescued mature INPs in nearly all btd mutant type II NB clones (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), expressing UAS-pntP1 failed to rescue mature INPs or suppress the ectopic nuclear Pros in Ase− immature INPs or Ase+ daughter cells in the majority of btd mutant clones (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from rescue experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In only 3 out of total 10 btd mutant clones expressing UAS-PntP1, mature INPs were partially rescued to 9.3 ± 3.2 per lineages.
source: Only in 3 out of total 10 btd mutant clones expressing UAS-PntP1, we observed that mature INPs were partially rescued to 9.3 ± 3.2 per lineages (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), which is still much fewer than the number of mature INPs (20–30 per lineages) in normal type II NB lineages.
evidence: This is quantitative data from rescue experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Btd mutant clones that did not show an obvious reduction of PntP1 in either the NBs or early immature INPs still failed to generate any mature INPs.
source: Consistent with the inability of UAS-pntP1 to fully rescue the loss of mature INPs, we found occasionally that btd mutant clones that did not show an obvious reduction of PntP1 in either the NBs or early immature INPs still failed to generate any mature INPs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observational data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The severe reduction/loss of PntP1 accounts for the ectopic Ase expression in btd mutant type II NBs but is not the primary reason for the loss of mature INPs.
source: Therefore, these results demonstrate that the severe reduction/loss of PntP1 accounts for the ectopic Ase expression in btd mutant type II NBs but is not the primary reason for the loss of mature INPs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments with PntP1 overexpression.

claim: PntP1 expression in both the NBs and immature INPs returned to normal levels when the loss of INPs was rescued by Pros RNAi knockdown in btd mutant type II NB clones.
source: Indeed, consistent with the suppression of the ectopic Ase expression by Pros RNAi knockdown, PntP1 expression in both the NBs and immature INPs returned to normal levels when the loss of INPs was rescued by Pros RNAi knockdown in btd mutant type II NB clones (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: This is observational and quantitative data shown in Figure 5D-F.

claim: The reduction/loss of PntP1 in btd mutant type II NB clones is due to the ectopic Pros expression in immature INPs.
source: These results suggest that the reduction/loss of PntP1 in btd mutant type II NB clones is due to the ectopic Pros expression in immature INPs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue of PntP1 expression when Pros is reduced.

claim: The reduction/loss of PntP1 and the subsequent ectopic Ase expression in the NB is most likely a secondary effect of the ectopic nuclear Pros expression in immature INPs.
source: However, given that ectopic nuclear Pros is only observed in immature INPs but not in the NBs in btd mutant type II NB clones, the reduction/loss of PntP1 and the subsequent ectopic Ase expression in the NB is most likely a secondary effect of the ectopic nuclear Pros expression in immature INPs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial pattern of Pros expression and PntP1 reduction.

claim: mCD8-GFP driven by the btd-GAL4 is expressed in all type II NB lineages but not type I NB lineages on the dorsal side of larval brains.
source: We found that mCD8-GFP driven by the btd-GAL4 is expressed in all type II NB lineages but not type I NB lineages on the dorsal side of larval brains (Figure 6A–A′).
evidence: This is observational data from btd-GAL4 reporter expression shown in Figure 6A-A'.

claim: In type II NB lineages, the expression of mCD8-GFP driven by btd-GAL4 is detected in the NB but becomes much stronger in immature INPs next to the NBs.
source: In type II NB lineages, the expression of mCD8-GFP driven by btd-GAL4 is detected in the NB but becomes much stronger in immature INPs next to the NBs (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is observational data from btd-GAL4 reporter expression shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The expression of mCD8-GFP driven by btd-GAL4 becomes progressively weak in cells away from the NBs and is barely detectable in some mature INPs distal from the NB.
source: The expression of mCD8-GFP then becomes progressively weak in cells away from the NBs and is barely detectable in some mature INPs distal from the NB (Figure 6A–A′).
evidence: This is observational data from btd-GAL4 reporter expression shown in Figure 6A-A'.

claim: mCD8-GFP driven by btd-GAL4 is expressed in two type I NB lineages on the ventral side of larval brains.
source: In addition to type II NB lineages, mCD8-GFP driven by btd-GAL4 is also expressed in two type I NB lineages on the ventral side of larval brains as well as about 31 type I NB lineages in the ventral nerve cord (VNC) (Figure 6B–C′).
evidence: This is observational data from btd-GAL4 reporter expression shown in Figure 6B-C'.

claim: mCD8-GFP driven by btd-GAL4 is expressed in about 31 type I NB lineages in the ventral nerve cord (VNC).
source: In addition to type II NB lineages, mCD8-GFP driven by btd-GAL4 is also expressed in two type I NB lineages on the ventral side of larval brains as well as about 31 type I NB lineages in the ventral nerve cord (VNC) (Figure 6B–C′).
evidence: This is observational data from btd-GAL4 reporter expression shown in Figure 6B-C'.

claim: The expression of UAS-mSp8 driven by btd-GAL4 fully rescued the loss of INPs resulting from Btd RNAi knockdown in all type II NB lineages.
source: As expected, the expression of UAS-mSp8 driven by btd-GAL4 fully rescued the loss of INPs resulting from Btd RNAi knockdown in all type II NB lineages (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is experimental rescue data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The expression of UAS-btd driven by btd-GAL4 partially rescued the loss of INPs in about 67% of lineages.
source: Similarly, the expression of UAS-btd driven by btd-GAL4 partially rescued the loss of INPs in about 67% of lineages (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is experimental rescue data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ectopic expression of PntP1 using btd-GAL4 as a driver induced the generation of INP-like cells in about 90% Btd-positive type I NB lineages in both larval brains and VNCs.
source: Interestingly, ectopic expression of PntP1 using btd-GAL4 as a driver induced the generation of INP-like cells in about 90% Btd-positive type I NB lineages in both larval brains (Figure 7A–C′,J) and VNCs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is quantitative data from ectopic expression experiments shown in Figure 7A-C', J and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The co-expression of UAS-pntP1 and UAS-btd driven by insc-GAL4 induced INP-like cells in about 95% of type I NB lineages in both larval brains and VNCs.
source: Consistently, the co-expression of UAS-pntP1 and UAS-btd driven by insc-GAL4 induced INP-like cells in about 95% of type I NB lineages in both larval brains and VNCs (Figure 7F–F′,I–I′,J, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is quantitative data from ectopic expression experiments shown in Figure 7F-I', J and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The expression of UAS-pntP1 alone driven by insc-GAL4 only induced INP-like cells in about 10% and 46% of type I NB lineages in larval brains and VNCs, respectively.
source: In contrast, the expression of UAS-pntP1 alone driven by insc-GAL4 only induced INP-like cells in about 10% and 46% of type I NB lineages in larval brains (Figure 7H–H′,J) and VNCs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), respectively, although ectopic PntP1 expression suppressed Ase in nearly all type I NBs (Figure 7H, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is quantitative data from ectopic expression experiments shown in Figure 7H-H', J and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The expression of UAS-btd alone neither suppressed Ase nor induced the generation of INP-like cells in VNCs.
source: The expression of UAS-btd alone neither suppressed Ase nor induced the generation of INP-like cells in VNCs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), whereas in larval brains, the expression of UAS-btd driven by insc-GAL4 suppressed/reduced the expression of Ase in the NB and promoted the generation of INP-like cells in about 20% of type I NB lineages (Figure 7G–G′,J).
evidence: This is observational data from ectopic expression experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The expression of UAS-btd driven by insc-GAL4 suppressed/reduced the expression of Ase in the NB and promoted the generation of INP-like cells in about 20% of type I NB lineages in larval brains.
source: The expression of UAS-btd alone neither suppressed Ase nor induced the generation of INP-like cells in VNCs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), whereas in larval brains, the expression of UAS-btd driven by insc-GAL4 suppressed/reduced the expression of Ase in the NB and promoted the generation of INP-like cells in about 20% of type I NB lineages (Figure 7G–G′,J).
evidence: This is quantitative data from ectopic expression experiments shown in Figure 7G-G', J.

claim: The generation of INPs requires the cooperative action of PntP1 and Btd.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the generation of INPs requires the cooperative action of PntP1 and Btd.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ectopic expression and loss-of-function experiments.

claim: The combination of Btd and PntP1 is sufficient to specify type II NB lineages and promote the generation of INPs.
source: Thus this study together with our previous work (Zhu et al., 2011) identified two key factors, PntP1 and Btd, a combination of which is sufficient to specify type II NB lineages and promote INP generation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current study and previous work (Zhu et al., 2011).

claim: There are 8 type II NBs in each brain lobe.
source: There are 8 type II NBs in each brain lobe.
evidence: This is a factual statement about Drosophila brain anatomy.

claim: Individual INPs undergo 4–6 rounds of asymmetric divisions to produce a new INP to self-renew and a ganglion mother cell (GMC), which divides terminally to produce neurons and/or glia.
source: Individual INPs undergo 4–6 rounds of asymmetric divisions to produce a new INP to self-renew and a ganglion mother cell (GMC), which divides terminally to produce neurons and/or glia (Bayraktar et al., 2010; Viktorin et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Bayraktar et al., 2010; Viktorin et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2013).

claim: Individual INPs produce distinct types of neurons by sequentially expressing a set of distinct transcription factors to specify the identity of their progeny.
source: Meanwhile, individual INPs produce distinct types of neurons by sequentially expressing a set of distinct transcription factors to specify the identity of their progeny (Bayraktar and Doe, 2013; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Bayraktar and Doe, 2013; Wang et al., 2014).

claim: Newly generated INPs are immature and do not express any NB markers, such as the proneural protein Asense (Ase) or the bHLH protein Deadpan (Dpn), except for Miranda (Mira).
source: Newly generated INPs are immature and do not express any NB markers, such as the proneural protein Asense (Ase) or the bHLH protein Deadpan (Dpn), except for Miranda (Mira).
evidence: This is a description of INP marker expression patterns.

claim: The Ase− immature INPs first turn on the expression of Ase to become Ase+ immature INPs.
source: The Ase− immature INPs first turn on the expression of Ase to become Ase+ immature INPs.
evidence: This describes the developmental progression of INPs.

claim: Ase+ immature INPs then further differentiate to become mature INPs, which express both Ase and Dpn.
source: Ase+ immature INPs then further differentiate to become mature INPs, which express both Ase and Dpn.
evidence: This describes the developmental progression of INPs.

claim: INPs do not divide until they are fully mature.
source: INPs do not divide until they are fully mature.
evidence: This is a statement about INP cell cycle behavior.

claim: The maturation of INPs requires Numb, the NHL family protein Brain tumor (Brat), the transcription factor Earmuff (Erm), as well as the BAP and Histone deacetylase 3 (HDAC3) chromatin remodeling complexes.
